Deuteronomy 1: Moses speaks east of the Jordan River on the plains of Moab, opposite Canaan, in the eleventh month of the fortieth year after the exodus (1:3). The text also lists wilderness landmarks (1:1-2) whose exact locations are uncertain. Dates in modern years are disputed: an earlier exodus date (around 1446 BC) and a later one (13th century BC) are both argued by scholars.
Deuteronomy 2: Moses recalls travel from Kadesh-barnea around Mount Seir and up the east side of the Dead Sea to the Arnon Valley (the border of Moab and the Amorite territory), then to Jahaz. The Transjordan was home to the emerging kingdoms of Edom, Moab, and Ammon. Exact dates and routes are not fixed by outside sources.
Deuteronomy 3: Bashan lay east of the Sea of Galilee and north of Gilead, a fertile plateau; Argob (3:4) is commonly linked to a volcanic basalt region there. Edrei, where Og was defeated, is generally placed near the modern Syria-Jordan border area. The identification of individual sites is not fully settled.
Deuteronomy 4: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab, looking back to Horeb (Sinai), where the covenant was made with the previous generation. The Baal-peor episode (4:3) occurred shortly before, in Numbers 25.
Deuteronomy 5: Moses addresses the new generation on the plains of Moab, recalling the giving of the Ten Commandments at Horeb (Exodus 20 gives the earlier account).
Deuteronomy 6: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab. The Shema belongs to this setting of final instruction before entering a land of established cities, vineyards, and wells.
Deuteronomy 7: Moses addresses Israel on the plains of Moab, just before crossing into Canaan. The seven nations represent peoples living in or near the land; exact identities and boundaries are not fully known.
Deuteronomy 8: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab, looking back on forty years in the wilderness and ahead to a fertile land.
Deuteronomy 9: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab. The golden calf episode occurred at Horeb after the Ten Commandments were given (Exodus 32-34).
Deuteronomy 10: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab, recalling events at Horeb and the journey that followed. Locations such as Moserah, Gudgodah, and Jotbathah are given but their exact sites are uncertain.
Deuteronomy 11: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab. Gerizim and Ebal are mountains near Shechem in the central hill country, west of the Jordan; the 'oaks of Moreh' (11:30) are in the same area.
Deuteronomy 12: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab. This chapter begins the 'statutes and rules' section (chapters 12-26), which applies the covenant to life in the land.
Deuteronomy 13: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab. Chapter 13 belongs to the statutes governing covenant loyalty.
Deuteronomy 14: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab. The dietary list parallels (Leviticus 11) with some differences.
Deuteronomy 15: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab. The seventh-year release is tied to the sabbatical cycle (see Exodus 21:2-6; 23:10-11; Leviticus 25).
Deuteronomy 16: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab. The month of Abib (16:1) is in spring, around the barley harvest.
Deuteronomy 17: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab, long before Israel had a king. The monarchy begins later, with Saul (1 Samuel 8-12).
Deuteronomy 18: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab. The prophet passage looks back to Horeb (5:22-27) and forward to Israel's life in the land.
Deuteronomy 19: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab. Three cities east of the Jordan were already designated in 4:41-43; the western cities are named in Joshua 20.
Deuteronomy 20: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab, shortly before the crossing of the Jordan and the campaigns later described in Joshua.
Deuteronomy 21: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab. These case laws apply the covenant to family and community life.
Deuteronomy 22: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab. The laws apply the covenant to daily life, from roofs and fields to marriage.
Deuteronomy 23: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab, with Israel encamped near Moabite territory. The Balaam and Baal-peor events (Numbers 22-25) belong to the recent past.
Deuteronomy 24: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab, applying the covenant to economic life and family relationships.
Deuteronomy 25: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab. The Amalek episode (Exodus 17) took place decades earlier, soon after the exodus.
Deuteronomy 26: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab. This chapter concludes the main body of the law (chapters 12-26).
Deuteronomy 27: Moses and the elders speak on the plains of Moab about a ceremony to be held later near Shechem, in the central hill country between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal. Joshua 8:30-35 describes it.
Deuteronomy 28: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab. Chapters 28-30 close the covenant with blessings, curses, and a call to choose.
Deuteronomy 29: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab. The Hebrew Bible numbers the first verse of this chapter as 28:69, so verse numbers differ from English Bibles by one throughout this chapter.
Deuteronomy 30: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab. Verses 1-10 describe a future situation of exile and return.
Deuteronomy 31: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab near the end of the fortieth year. The seventh-year reading at Booths is tied to the year of release (see 15:1-2).
Deuteronomy 32: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab. Mount Nebo is in the Abarim range, overlooking the plains and the land west of the Jordan; it is traditionally identified with a ridge in modern Jordan.
Deuteronomy 33: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab shortly before his death. The poem uses archaic Hebrew and some verses are hard to translate.
Deuteronomy 34: The scene is Mount Nebo/Pisgah in Moab, east of the Jordan and opposite Jericho, at the end of the fortieth year. The exact burial valley is unknown.
Joshua 1: The scene is the plains of Moab, east of the Jordan River and opposite Jericho, at Shittim (see 2:1; 3:1). It follows directly after the death of Moses (Deuteronomy 34). Dates in modern years are disputed: some scholars favor an earlier timeline (conquest around 1400 BC) and others a later one (13th century BC). The earliest known non-biblical mention of 'Israel' as a people in Canaan is the Merneptah Stele from Egypt (about 1208 BC).
Joshua 2: Shittim (also called Abel-shittim) lies on the plains of Moab east of the Jordan; Jericho is a walled city just west of the river, in the Jordan Valley. The site is commonly identified with Tell es-Sultan. Canaan in the Late Bronze Age was a collection of city-states, as reflected in the Amarna letters from Egypt (14th century BC).
Joshua 3: The crossing takes place near Jericho in the spring, when the Jordan overflows during the barley harvest (3:15; compare 4:19, which dates it to the tenth day of the first month). Adam (3:16) is a town upstream, generally identified with Tell ed-Damiyeh, about 16 miles (25 km) north of Jericho, though the identification is not certain.
Joshua 4: Gilgal is described as east of Jericho (4:19), on the tenth day of the first month. Its exact site is uncertain, and several locations have been proposed. The tenth day of the first month matches the day the Passover lamb was set aside in Exodus 12:3, which sets up the Passover in chapter 5.
Joshua 5: Israel is camped at Gilgal near Jericho. The wilderness generation had died, and the new generation had not undergone the covenant sign of circumcision according to the text (5:5).
Joshua 6: Jericho (Tell es-Sultan) is one of the oldest continuously inhabited sites in the world, in the Jordan Valley. The date of Jericho's fall depends on the date of the conquest. Archaeological evidence is debated: Kathleen Kenyon dated Jericho's last major Bronze Age destruction to about 1550 BC, while others, such as John Garstang and Bryant Wood, argued for a destruction around 1400 BC. Erosion has removed much of the later Bronze Age city, and scholars disagree on how to interpret the evidence.
Joshua 7: The story takes place near Jericho and the hill country to the west. Ai (meaning 'the ruin') is located near Bethel (7:2). Its exact location is debated; candidates include et-Tell, Khirbet el-Maqatir, and others. The Valley of Achor lies near Jericho.
Joshua 8: Ai lies in the central hill country near Bethel. Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim overlook Shechem, about 20 miles (30 km) north of Ai, where Moses had commanded a ceremony (Deuteronomy 11:29–30; 27:1–8).
Joshua 9: Gibeon is about 6 miles (10 km) northwest of Jerusalem, generally identified with el-Jib. Excavations there uncovered a large water system and wine-making installations, along with jar handles inscribed with 'Gibeon' (gb'n) from the Iron Age. These discoveries support the location but do not date or confirm the treaty itself.
Joshua 10: The battle begins at Gibeon and moves west and south through the Valley of Aijalon, Beth-horon, Azekah, and Makkedah, then to Lachish, Eglon, Hebron, and Debir. These are in the hill country and Shephelah of what became Judah. The Amarna letters (14th century BC) show Jerusalem ruled by a local king, Abdi-Heba, who was a vassal of Egypt, illustrating that city-state kings existed in this area, though they do not refer to Joshua.
Joshua 11: Hazor was in Galilee, north of the Sea of Galilee, and the waters of Merom are in the same region. Tel Hazor (Tell el-Qedah) has been extensively excavated by Yigael Yadin and later Amnon Ben-Tor and was the largest Canaanite city in the area. Archaeology shows Hazor was destroyed by fire in the 13th century BC. Scholars disagree on who destroyed it: Israelites, Egyptians, the Sea Peoples, or a local conflict.
Joshua 12: The list covers the Transjordan, the Jordan Valley, the hill country, the Shephelah, and the coast and plains in the north. Canaan was divided among many small city-states, a pattern known from the Amarna letters (14th century BC).
Joshua 13: The chapter looks across the whole region, from the Philistine coastal plain in the southwest to Lebanon in the north and the Transjordan highlands in the east. Joshua is described as 'old and advanced in years' (13:1). The Philistines are archaeologically visible on the southern coast from around the early 12th century BC, and how that evidence fits with the dating of Joshua is debated.
Joshua 14: The setting is Gilgal, near Jericho (14:6), where Judah's representatives approach Joshua. Hebron lies in the hill country of Judah, south of Jerusalem, and is identified with Tell Rumeida, though the identification of the ancient town is debated. According to the text, the spies' report was given at Kadesh-barnea (Numbers 13-14), when Caleb was forty, and the year is now when he is eighty-five (14:7,10).
Joshua 15: Judah's allotment covered the southern hill country, the Shephelah, the Negeb, and the wilderness near the Dead Sea. Jerusalem lay on its northern border. The boundary descriptions read like land documents, and the town lists have been compared by scholars to administrative lists, possibly from a later period such as the monarchy; this is debated. The location of Debir (Kiriath-sepher) is uncertain, with Khirbet Rabud and Tell Beit Mirsim among proposals.
Joshua 16: The territory covers the central hill country north of Benjamin and Judah, including Bethel and the area around Shechem and later Shiloh. Gezer, on the western edge of the hill country, controlled a route to the coast. Gezer is mentioned on the Merneptah Stele (about 1208 BC) as a city captured by Egypt, which shows Egypt's interest in the region. In 1 Kings 9:16 an Egyptian pharaoh gives Gezer to Solomon's wife.
Joshua 17: Manasseh's western portion was in the central hill country north of Ephraim, bordering the Jezreel Valley and the coastal plain, with cities such as Beth-shean, Ibleam, Dor, Taanach, and Megiddo. Archaeology shows many small new highland villages appeared across the central hill country in the early Iron Age (about 1200-1000 BC), though scholars debate who the settlers were and where they came from.
Joshua 18: Shiloh is in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Bethel. Excavations at Khirbet Seilun show an Iron Age I settlement destroyed around the 11th century BC, which is consistent with the later references to Shiloh's destruction (see Jeremiah 7:12-14), though the dating is debated. Benjamin's territory lies between Judah and Ephraim and includes Jericho, Bethel, Gibeon, and Jerusalem's northern border.
Joshua 19: The tribes now settle across the Galilee, Jezreel Valley, coastal regions, and southern hill country. Dan's move to Leshem (called Laish in Judges 18) is placed in the narrative here as an anticipation, and the full account is in Judges 17-18. Tel Dan in northern Israel has been extensively excavated, though the connection to the biblical account is debated.
Joshua 20: The six cities are spread across the land: Kedesh in the north, Shechem in the center, and Hebron in the south in the west; Bezer, Ramoth-gilead, and Golan in the east. Their locations meant that a refuge was within a day's travel from most places.
Joshua 21: The Levitical cities were spread throughout the tribes, from Galilee to the Negeb and east of the Jordan. The list parallels (1 Chronicles 6:54-81). Scholars debate whether this system was fully implemented historically or reflects an ideal scheme; the text presents it as carried out.
Joshua 22: The altar is built near the Jordan 'in the land of Canaan' at a place called Geliloth (22:10-11), whose exact location is uncertain. Shiloh is the central sanctuary. The eastern tribes live beyond the Jordan, which was itself a natural boundary between the two groups.
Joshua 23: The speech is set some time after the allotment, when Joshua is old; the text does not say where, though it is often placed near Shiloh or Timnath-serah. Its themes echo Moses' farewell in Deuteronomy 31-33. According to 24:29, Joshua died at 110.
Joshua 24: Shechem lies in the hill country of Ephraim between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, and is identified with Tell Balata. It had earlier links to Abraham (Genesis 12:6–7) and Jacob (Genesis 33:18–20). The Hebrew text says the people assembled at Shechem, while some Greek manuscripts read Shiloh. The speech follows the form of ancient treaties, beginning with a historical review.
Judges 1: After Joshua's death, the tribes fight separately for their territories, and many Canaanite towns remain (Judges 1:27–33). Judges covers the time before Israel had a king, usually placed in the early Iron Age, about 1200–1050 BC.
Judges 2: A new generation grows up "which knew not the LORD" (Judges 2:10). The chapter sets out the cycle that repeats through the book: idolatry, oppression, crying out, and a deliverer.
Judges 3: Othniel defeats Chushanrishathaim of Mesopotamia; Ehud kills Eglon king of Moab at Jericho, "the city of palm trees" (Judges 3:13); Shamgar fights the Philistines.
Judges 4: Jabin king of Canaan rules from Hazor, with Sisera commanding nine hundred iron chariots (Judges 4:3). Deborah judges under a palm tree between Ramah and Bethel.
Judges 5: Deborah and Barak's song celebrates the victory by the river Kishon. It is often considered among the oldest poetry in the Bible.
Judges 6: Midianites and Amalekites raid Israel at harvest for seven years, camels and all (Judges 6:3–5). Gideon threshes wheat in a winepress at Ophrah to hide it.
Judges 7: Gideon camps by the well of Harod with three hundred men; the Midianites lie in the valley below the hill of Moreh, in the Jezreel valley.
Judges 8: Gideon pursues the Midianite kings east across the Jordan to Succoth and Penuel, then returns to Ophrah. The land has rest forty years (Judges 8:28).
Judges 9: Gideon's son Abimelech makes himself king at Shechem for three years and dies attacking the tower of Thebez.
Judges 10: Tola and Jair judge Israel. The Ammonites oppress Gilead, east of the Jordan, for eighteen years (Judges 10:8).
Judges 11: Jephthah of Gilead fights Ammon. He says Israel has held the land for three hundred years (Judges 11:26).
Judges 12: Ephraim fights Jephthah's Gileadites at the Jordan fords, where the password "Shibboleth" exposes the Ephraimites (Judges 12:6).
Judges 13: The Philistines rule Israel for forty years (Judges 13:1). Samson is born to Manoah of Zorah, a Danite town in the foothills bordering Philistine land.
Judges 14: Samson goes down to Timnath to marry a Philistine woman. Timnah has been identified with Tel Batash in the Sorek valley.
Judges 15: Samson burns Philistine grain at harvest and kills a thousand men at Ramathlehi in Judah.
Judges 16: Samson visits Gaza, falls to Delilah in the valley of Sorek, and dies in the temple of Dagon at Gaza. He judged Israel twenty years (Judges 16:31).
Judges 17: "In those days there was no king in Israel" (Judges 17:6). Micah of mount Ephraim sets up a shrine and hires a Levite from Bethlehem.
Judges 18: The Danites, still without land, move north and take Laish, renaming it Dan. Tel Dan, near the sources of the Jordan, has been excavated.
Judges 19: A Levite travels from Bethlehem with his concubine and stays at Gibeah in Benjamin, a few miles north of Jerusalem, which was then "Jebus" (Judges 19:10).
Judges 20: The tribes gather at Mizpeh and fight Benjamin at Gibeah. The ark of the covenant is at Bethel "in those days" (Judges 20:27), with Phinehas, Aaron's grandson, as priest.
Judges 21: The tribes find wives for Benjamin's survivors from Jabeshgilead and from the yearly feast at Shiloh.
Ruth 1: The story is set "in the days when the judges ruled" (Ruth 1:1). Elimelech's family moves from Bethlehem in Judah to Moab, east of the Dead Sea, during a famine.
Ruth 2: Ruth gleans in Boaz's field near Bethlehem from the barley harvest through the wheat harvest (Ruth 2:23), roughly April to June.
Ruth 3: Boaz winnows barley at night on the threshing floor at Bethlehem (Ruth 3:2).
Ruth 4: Boaz settles the matter before ten elders at Bethlehem's gate. The book ends with a genealogy from Pharez to David (Ruth 4:18–22).
